query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEAs, the metastable microstructure evolves via diffusion‐driven coarsening and segregation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases—especially at grain boundaries—thereby altering the local chemistry so that high-temperature exposures induce the formation of more continuous, adherent oxide scales (e.g., MgO) while at the same time disrupting the uniform passivation necessary for optimal corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, homogenized lightweight HEA (density <6 g/cm3) exhibiting a metastable mixture of a solid-solution matrix with finely dispersed intermetallic compounds (including Mg-rich phases).
generation.intervention: Subjecting one set of otherwise identical alloys to a controlled annealing treatment (or exposure to sustained high-temperature conditions) to promote microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: Processing via induction melting under non-equilibrium conditions; subsequent annealing at temperatures below the incipient melting point, with oxidation performed under high-temperature air or oxygen-rich atmospheres and corrosion assessed in a standardized electrolyte (e.g., NaCl solution).
generation.structural_mediator: The coarsening and grain-boundary segregation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases that modify the local elemental composition at the surface and near-surface regions.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated diffusion during annealing causes Mg and other elements to segregate, leading to the coarsening of intermetallic compounds. This change in local chemistry facilitates the preferential formation of a continuous oxide layer (such as MgO) during high-temperature oxidation while simultaneously creating chemically heterogeneous regions that interfere with the formation of a uniform passive film during corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, annealed samples will show thicker and more adherent high-temperature oxide scales (indicating enhanced oxidation resistance) and a modified electrochemical response—likely manifesting as higher or more variable corrosion current densities due to disrupted passivation.
generation.baseline: The initial, non-equilibrium microstructure established by induction melting, characterized by a fine solid-solution matrix with a homogeneous dispersion of small intermetallic precipitates.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected for lightweight HEAs processed under induction melting and annealing below their incipient melting point; significant deviations in alloy composition outside the studied Mg-containing system or processing conditions (e.g., extreme annealing temperatures) may lead to different evolution pathways.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative changes in corrosion current density and oxide scale thickness/adherence are not precisely predicted and will depend on specific Mg content, annealing parameters, and testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples via induction melting. Subject one set to a controlled annealing treatment designed to promote phase evolution, while leaving the other set in the as-cast condition. Characterize both sets with high-resolution microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess the distribution and coarsening of Mg-rich intermetallics. Perform high-temperature oxidation tests (evaluating oxide scale thickness and adherence) and standardized corrosion tests (measuring corrosion current densities via electrochemical polarization).
measurements: Intermetallic phase size and grain-boundary Mg segregation via microscopy/EDS
Oxide scale thickness and integrity after high-temperature oxidation tests
Corrosion current densities and passivation quality from electrochemical measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit significant coarsening or segregation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases relative to the as-cast baseline, or if the observed changes in oxidation and corrosion performance do not correlate with the predicted microstructural changes (i.e., no enhanced oxide scale formation or altered corrosion behavior), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One promising design strategy involves the development of multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), which incorporate multiple elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios to achieve property combinations beyond those achievable in conventional binary or ternary systems. While this concept has been widely explored in high-entropy alloys, its application to Mg-rich systems remains limited and may offer new pathways for improving corrosion resistance, mechanical performance, and maintaining a low density. While prior studies have investigated Mg-Ti, Mg-Zn, and Zn-Ti binary alloys individually, the combined effects of Ti and Zn in bulk Mg-rich multi-element systems remain poorly understood, particularly with respect to phase stability, passivation behavior, and mechanical properties.

Lightweight complex concentrated alloys (LWCCA), composed of elements with low density, have become a great area of interest due to the high demand in a large number of applications. Previous research on LWCCAs was focused on high entropy multicomponent alloy systems that provide low density and high capability of solid solution formation. Present research introduces two alloy systems (Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si) that contain readily available and inexpensive starting materials and have potential for solid solution formation structures. For the selection of appropriate compositions, authors applied semi-empirical criteria and optimization software. Specialized modeling software (MatCalc) was used to determine probable alloy structures by CALPHAD, non-equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations. The selected alloys were prepared in an induction furnace. Specimens were heat treated to provide stable structures. Physicochemical, microstructural, and mechanical characterization was performed for the selected alloy compositions.
